blocks.text:
After breakfast, head to Corcovado. The train climbs through the Tijuca Forest. As you gain altitude, the city disappears behind the greenery, then comes back into view from the upper observation area.

The statue of Christ the Redeemer stands on the summit. Up close, the monumental figure draws your attention first; then the panorama takes over: Guanabara Bay, the Maracanã Stadium, the Botanical Garden, Sugar Loaf, beaches and neighbourhoods nestled between the mountains.

After Sugar Loaf, this is Rio’s second great panoramic viewpoint, but from a different angle. Together, the two excursions help you understand the city’s geography and the location of its main districts.

In the evening, you may head to the rocks of Arpoador to watch the sunset. Another option is dinner at the seafood restaurant Marius, around USD 130 per person.

The pace is noticeably gentler after Carnival night. The train passes through the forest, followed by time at the viewing area and the journey back. Sunset at Arpoador can remain a free-time extension of the day, rather than a compulsory group activity. This pause is particularly welcome before the flight to Iguazu.

blocks.text:
After breakfast, transfer to the airport for your flight to Foz do Iguaçu. On arrival, you will be met and transferred to your selected hotel.

The flight takes you from the Carnival atmosphere to Brazil’s natural wonders in a single day. In the morning, you are still in Rio, where beaches, mountains and urban neighbourhoods define the landscape. By the time you reach Iguazu, tropical greenery is much more prominent. The main sightseeing programme starts the next day, leaving you free to settle into your hotel after travelling.

The character of the trip changes after Rio. The national park lies within a humid tropical forest. Even before you reach the main viewing platforms, you may hear the low roar of the water and see a white cloud of spray rising above the trees.

Over the following two days, you will experience the falls from both sides. The Brazilian side offers broad panoramic views of the cascades, while the Argentine side brings you closer to individual streams and along walkways above the river.

Compared with Rio, the urban setting almost disappears. Most of the routes run through national parks, among damp forest, walkways and viewpoints. You hear the falls first; then individual white torrents appear between the trees, before much of the vast waterfall system finally comes into view. This gradual approach makes the first day at Iguazu a memorable experience in itself, not merely a stop between flights.
